key_terms.meaning: A combinational block that adds three input bits a, b, cᵢₙ and gives sum s = a ⊕ b ⊕ cᵢₙ and carry cₒᵤₜ = ab + bcᵢₙ + acᵢₙ.
g = a·b (this bit makes a carry) and p = a ⊕ b (this bit passes an incoming carry on).
N full adders chained so each carry enters the next stage; the delay grows linearly with N.
Adder that computes carries directly from g and p with two-level AND-OR logic instead of waiting for them to ripple.
G = g₃ + p₃g₂ + p₃p₂g₁ + p₃p₂p₁g₀ and P = p₃p₂p₁p₀, which let a 4-bit block be treated as one big bit.
Two copies of a block compute with carry-in 0 and 1; a multiplexer picks the right sum when the real carry arrives.
A row of full adders that adds three numbers and produces sum and carry vectors without resolving carries, so the carry is delayed, not rippled.
Blocks whose propagate bits are ANDed into one block propagate P; when P = 1 a multiplexer sends the incoming carry straight past the block.
One row of the multiplication table, formed as aᵢ · B, that is shifted left by i bit positions before adding.
Unsigned array multiplier: n² AND gates and n(n−1) adder cells (n(n−2) full adders, n half adders) in a fixed, regular layout.
Two's complement array multiplier that keeps the regular array shape and fixes sign by inverting some partial product bits and adding two correction constants.
Adder tree that reduces many partial product rows to two using layers of 3:2 counters, so delay grows as log of the number of rows.
A full adder used as a counter: it takes three bits of equal weight and outputs two bits of weights 2 and 1, reducing the row count by one.
Rewriting the multiplier as signed digits: radix-2 reads bit pairs (digits −1, 0, +1); radix-4 reads overlapping triplets (digits −2 to +2) and halves the number of partial products.
A circuit with n inputs and 2ⁿ outputs where exactly one output is active for each input code; the minterm generator of combinational logic.
A circuit that passes one of 2ⁿ data inputs to a single output under the control of n select bits.
A circuit that compares two n-bit words and asserts equal, greater-than or less-than using cascaded equality and magnitude signals.
A storage element that copies D to Q while its clock is active (high for a positive latch) and holds the last value otherwise; Q = CLK·D + CLK′·Q.
Data must be stable for tₛᵤ before the clock edge and tₕ after it; violating either can make the register store a wrong or metastable value.
Two cross-coupled CMOS inverters plus two access transistors; it holds a bit as long as power is on and needs no refresh.
One access transistor and one capacitor storing charge; the bit leaks away and must be refreshed every few milliseconds.
A negative latch followed by a positive latch on the same clock; Q changes only just after the rising edge. T ≥ t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>comb,max</sub> + t<sub>su</sub>.
Dynamic registers built from clocked inverters: C<sup>2</sup>MOS is insensitive to clock overlap; TSPC needs only one clock phase.
Registers placed inside long logic: T<sub>pipe</sub> = t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>stage,max</sub> + t<sub>su</sub>; throughput 1 ÷ T<sub>pipe</sub>; latency k × T<sub>pipe</sub>.
Inverter with two thresholds V<sub>M+</sub> > V<sub>M−</sub>; hysteresis V<sub>H</sub> = V<sub>M+</sub> − V<sub>M−</sub> rejects noise smaller than V<sub>H</sub>.
An odd number N of inverters in a loop; f = 1 ÷ (2N·t<sub>p</sub>).
Setup: T + δ ≥ t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>logic</sub> + t<sub>su</sub> + 2t<sub>jit</sub>. Hold: t<sub>cq,cd</sub> + t<sub>logic,cd</sub> ≥ t<sub>h</sub> + δ + 2t<sub>jit</sub>.
Output goes to 1 when both inputs are 1, to 0 when both are 0, and holds otherwise; the joining element of self-timed handshakes.
ΔV = (V<sub>cell</sub> − V<sub>DD</sub>/2) × C<sub>S</sub> ÷ (C<sub>S</sub> + C<sub>BL</sub>); tens of millivolts, so the read is sensed and then restored.
N = 2<sup>K</sup> words of M bits in 2<sup>r</sup> rows of M × 2<sup>c</sup> columns, with K = r + c; predecoded row decoder, column multiplexer and sense amplifiers.
A cross-coupled latch fired by sense enable once the bitline difference is large enough; it saves the time t = C<sub>BL</sub>ΔV ÷ I<sub>cell</sub> of a full swing.

takeaways: A wide adder is a carry problem: ripple carry settles in about 2n gate delays, and every faster adder is a different way to tell the top bits their carry sooner.
Carry look-ahead computes every carry from generate and propagate terms in two-level logic; blocks of 4 bits with group generate and propagate keep the gates small and the delay logarithmic.

Carry select precomputes both answers, carry skip bypasses blocks whose bits all propagate (best block size √(n·t<sub>mux</sub> ÷ 2t<sub>c</sub>)), and carry save postpones the carry to one final adder.
An array multiplier is regular but its delay grows linearly with n; Baugh-Wooley handles two's complement in the same array with 2(n−1) inverted bits and two correction 1s.
A Wallace tree reduces partial-product rows with 3:2 counters in logarithmic depth, and radix-4 Booth recoding halves the rows it has to reduce.
A latch is level-sensitive and a master-slave register is edge-triggered; setup uses the longest path and the clock period, hold uses the shortest path and never contains T.
Pipelining raises throughput, not speed per item: latency grows, and k stages give less than k times the rate because of register overhead and unbalanced stages.
Skew helps one timing check and hurts the other, jitter only hurts; self-timed design replaces the clock with handshakes, completion detection and C-elements.
An SRAM bit lives in a feedback loop and a DRAM bit in leaking charge read as a tens-of-millivolts swing; ROM stores bits as present or absent transistors.
A memory is a square core plus periphery: K = r + c address bits, predecoded row decoders, column multiplexers, sense amplifiers and timing control set its speed.
bank_note: Long answers are marked on the circuit or block diagram, the delay or timing expression worked with numbers, and a clear area-versus-speed verdict, so sketch first and then justify the numbers. Most syllabi ask for the adder and multiplier architectures with their delay, the latch and register circuits with setup and hold, and the memory cell with its read and write operation.

bank.q: Draw the transistor-level CMOS full adder and write its sum and carry functions. Build a 4-bit ripple carry adder from it and explain why its delay grows with the word length.
outline: Sum = a ⊕ b ⊕ c<sub>in</sub>, carry = ab + c<sub>in</sub>(a ⊕ b)
The 28-transistor mirror adder: carry gate, sum gate reusing C̄<sub>out</sub>, two inverters
4-bit chain: c<sub>out</sub> of each stage is the c<sub>in</sub> of the next
Worst case: carry born at bit 0; c<sub>n</sub> at 2n gate delays, top sum bit at 2n − 1
Area grows linearly; delay grows linearly with n
answer: Full adder functions. For inputs a, b and carry-in c: S = a ⊕ b ⊕ c and C<sub>out</sub> = ab + c(a ⊕ b), which equals the majority function ab + bc + ca. A carry leaves when both inputs are 1, or when exactly one is 1 and a carry came in.

answer.text: Truth table (the check for any circuit you draw):

answer: Transistor-level cell. The standard static CMOS cell is the 28-transistor mirror adder. Its carry gate forms C̄<sub>out</sub> directly: nMOS network a·b in parallel with c·(a + b), and a pMOS network of the same series-parallel shape (the "mirror"), 10 transistors. Its sum gate forms S̄ from S = abc + C̄<sub>out</sub>(a + b + c), 14 transistors. Two output inverters (4 transistors) restore S and C<sub>out</sub>: 10 + 14 + 4 = 28.

Check the sum gate against the table: when the majority is 1 (C̄<sub>out</sub> = 0), S = abc, so S = 1 only for 111; when the majority is 0, at most one input is 1 and S = a + b + c. Both match the table.

Drawing. Draw the carry gate first (its output C̄<sub>out</sub> feeds the sum gate), label V<sub>DD</sub>, ground, a, b, c, C̄<sub>out</sub> and S̄, then the two output inverters. Because the sum gate waits for C̄<sub>out</sub>, the carry is always ready before the sum.

4-bit ripple carry adder. Connect four cells in a row: bit i of a and b enters cell i, and C<sub>out</sub> of cell i drives c<sub>in</sub> of cell i + 1. c<sub>0</sub> = 0 for addition; for subtraction XOR each b bit with a control line and set c<sub>0</sub> = 1, since a − b = a + b̄ + 1.

answer.text: Timing with 2 gate delays per carry stage and one XOR for each sum, worst case (carry born at bit 0, for example a = 1111, b = 0001):

answer: Why the delay grows. Each stage must wait for the carry of the stage below, so the carry path passes every cell: t<sub>carry</sub> = 2n and the top sum bit settles at 2n − 1 gate delays, linear in n. For n = 32 that is 64 gate delays, 2.56 ns at 40 ps per gate, which is too slow for a 1 GHz clock.

Area and layout. One cell is repeated n times: 28n transistors (112 for 4 bits), with short regular wiring. This makes ripple carry the smallest adder and the right choice for small or slow datapaths; faster adders (look-ahead, select, skip) shorten the carry path at the cost of area.
Check: 1111 + 0001 = 10000 (15 + 1 = 16). Every column has p = 1 except bit 0, which generates, so the carry really does walk all four stages and c<sub>4</sub> = 1 arrives last, at 8 gate delays.

bank.q: Define carry generate and carry propagate for one bit. Derive the carry expressions c₁ to c₄ for a 4-bit carry look-ahead adder and explain what limits block size.
outline: g<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>i</sub>, p<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub> ⊕ b<sub>i</sub>
c<sub>i+1</sub> = g<sub>i</sub> + p<sub>i</sub>c<sub>i</sub> expanded for each stage
Two-level AND-OR realisation: all carries in about 3 gate delays
Fan-in and gate count grow with block width
Group generate and propagate cascade 4-bit blocks: 16 bits in about 8 gate delays
answer: Definitions. Generate g<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>i</sub>: column i makes a carry by itself. Propagate p<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub> ⊕ b<sub>i</sub>: column i passes an incoming carry on. Both depend only on that column's own bits, so all of them are ready after one gate delay. (Some texts use p<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub> + b<sub>i</sub>; it works for carries, but then the sum must be written a<sub>i</sub> ⊕ b<sub>i</sub> ⊕ c<sub>i</sub>.)

Recurrence. A carry leaves column i if the column generates one, or if it propagates and a carry came in: c<sub>i+1</sub> = g<sub>i</sub> + p<sub>i</sub>c<sub>i</sub>, and the sum is s<sub>i</sub> = p<sub>i</sub> ⊕ c<sub>i</sub>.

answer.text: Substitute each carry into the next so that no carry depends on another:
answer.pre:
c₁ = g₀ + p₀c₀
c₂ = g₁ + p₁c₁ = g₁ + p₁g₀ + p₁p₀c₀
c₃ = g₂ + p₂c₂ = g₂ + p₂g₁ + p₂p₁g₀ + p₂p₁p₀c₀
c₄ = g₃ + p₃c₃ = g₃ + p₃g₂ + p₃p₂g₁ + p₃p₂p₁g₀ + p₃p₂p₁p₀c₀

answer: Realisation. Each carry is now a sum of products of g, p and c<sub>0</sub>: one AND level and one OR level. The look-ahead carry unit builds all four at once, so the carries are ready about 3 gate delays after the inputs (1 for g and p, 2 for AND-OR) and the sums one XOR later, at 4, against 8 for a 4-bit ripple adder.

answer.text: Trace for a = 1011, b = 0110, c<sub>0</sub> = 0:

answer: From the expansions: c<sub>2</sub> = g<sub>1</sub> = 1; c<sub>3</sub> = p<sub>2</sub>g<sub>1</sub> = 1; c<sub>4</sub> = p<sub>3</sub>p<sub>2</sub>g<sub>1</sub> = 1·1·1 = 1. Result c<sub>4</sub>s<sub>3</sub>s<sub>2</sub>s<sub>1</sub>s<sub>0</sub> = 10001 = 17 = 11 + 6.

What limits block size. The term for c<sub>n</sub> contains p<sub>n−1</sub>…p<sub>0</sub>c<sub>0</sub>, an AND of n + 1 inputs, and c<sub>n</sub> is an OR of n + 1 terms. In static CMOS a wide gate means a long series stack (slow, large) or a tree of gates (more levels), and the low-order g and p signals fan out to every later carry. Beyond about 4 bits the "constant" delay is lost, so practical blocks are 4 bits.

Wider adders. Each 4-bit block also produces a group generate G = g<sub>3</sub> + p<sub>3</sub>g<sub>2</sub> + p<sub>3</sub>p<sub>2</sub>g<sub>1</sub> + p<sub>3</sub>p<sub>2</sub>p<sub>1</sub>g<sub>0</sub> and a group propagate P = p<sub>3</sub>p<sub>2</sub>p<sub>1</sub>p<sub>0</sub>. A second-level unit treats each block as one big bit: C<sub>4</sub> = G<sub>0</sub> + P<sub>0</sub>c<sub>0</sub>, and so on.

answer.text: Gate-delay budget of a 16-bit two-level look-ahead adder:

head: Step
Ready after
rows: block carries C<sub>4</sub>, C<sub>8</sub>, C<sub>12</sub> from the second level

answer: Check: about 8 gate delays for 16 bits against 2 × 16 = 32 for ripple; each added level of look-ahead adds about 4 gate delays while multiplying the width by 4, which is the logarithmic growth.

bank.q: Explain with block diagrams how a carry select adder, a carry save adder and a carry skip adder each reduce the effect of the carry chain.
outline: Carry select: duplicate blocks for c<sub>in</sub> = 0 and 1, multiplexers select
Multiplexer delay replaces the ripple through each block; square-root block sizes
Carry save: three operands to two vectors, carry postponed to one final CPA
Carry skip: block propagate (AND of the p bits) drives a bypass multiplexer
Comparison of area overhead and delay gain
answer: The problem. In a ripple adder the carry must pass every bit, so the delay grows as 2n gate delays. The three adders attack this in three different ways: compute both answers early (select), postpone the carry (save), or jump over blocks that would only pass it on (skip).

Carry select, block diagram. Split the adder into blocks. In every block except the first, draw two ripple adders on the same a and b bits, one with carry-in 0 and one with carry-in 1, and a row of 2:1 multiplexers (one per sum bit plus one for the block carry-out). The real carry from the block below drives the select lines.

Carry select, worked. For a = 1011, b = 0110 in 2-bit blocks: the low block gives 01 with carry 1; the high block gives 11, carry 0 (for c<sub>in</sub> = 0) and 00, carry 1 (for c<sub>in</sub> = 1). The real carry 1 selects 1 00, so the sum is 10001 = 17. Both high answers were ready before the carry arrived; only one multiplexer delay was added.

Carry select, delay and area. With equal blocks of k bits the delay is about k carry delays plus n/k − 1 multiplexer delays. Making each block one bit longer than the one below (2, 3, 4 …) lets each block finish just as its select arrives, so the delay grows roughly as √(2n) multiplexer delays. Area is nearly double a ripple adder plus the multiplexers.

answer.text: Carry save, block diagram and worked example: one row of full adders, one per column, takes three numbers a, b, d and gives a sum word S and a carry word C shifted one place left. For a = 1011, b = 0110, d = 0101:

answer: S = 1000 = 8 and the raw carries 0111 shifted left give C = 1110 = 14. One carry propagate adder then gives 8 + 14 = 22 = 11 + 6 + 5. The CSA row has the delay of one full adder whatever the width, because no carry crosses a column; only the final adder ripples. It is the building block of multi-operand adders and multiplier trees.

Carry skip, block diagram. Keep a ripple adder in each block of k bits, and add an AND gate forming the block propagate P = p<sub>m</sub>·p<sub>m+1</sub>·…·p<sub>m+k−1</sub> and a 2:1 multiplexer on the block carry-out. If P = 1 every bit would pass the carry, so the multiplexer sends c<sub>in</sub> straight to the next block; if P = 0 the block either generates or kills its carry, and the normal ripple carry-out is used. It must be an AND: one p<sub>i</sub> = 0 stops the bypass.

Carry skip, delay. Worst case: generated in the first block, ripples k bits, skips the middle blocks, ripples k bits in the last: T ≈ 2k·t<sub>c</sub> + (n/k − 1)·t<sub>mux</sub>, best at k = √(n·t<sub>mux</sub> ÷ 2t<sub>c</sub>). For 32 bits with t<sub>c</sub> = t<sub>mux</sub> = 1: k = 4 gives 8 + 7 = 15 units against 32 for ripple.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Adder
How it beats the chain
Extra hardware
Delay (32 bits, rough)
rows: one AND and one multiplexer per block

answer: Verdict: carry skip is the cheapest speed-up, carry select the faster but larger one, and carry save is not a complete adder but the right tool whenever three or more numbers must be added.

bank.q: Describe the 6T SRAM cell and the 1T1C DRAM cell. Compare them on area per bit, speed, retention and refresh requirement.
outline: 6T: two cross-coupled inverters plus two access transistors
Read with bitlines precharged to V<sub>DD</sub>; cell ratio for read stability, pull-up ratio for write
1T1C: one transistor plus a capacitor; charge sharing with the bitline
Destructive read and leakage force restore and refresh
DRAM is denser and cheaper per bit, SRAM is faster and needs no refresh
answer: 6T SRAM structure. Two cross-coupled CMOS inverters (four transistors) hold Q and Q̄ in a bistable loop. Two nMOS access transistors, gated by the wordline WL, connect Q to bitline BL and Q̄ to BLB. Draw the loop in the middle, the access transistors at the sides, WL across the top and BL, BLB down the sides.

SRAM read. Precharge BL and BLB to V<sub>DD</sub>, then raise WL. The side storing 0 pulls its bitline down slowly through the access and pull-down transistors; the sense amplifier detects a difference of about 0.1 V. The read is non-destructive, but the low node rises a little because the access and pull-down transistors form a divider. A cell ratio (pull-down W/L ÷ access W/L) above about 1.2 keeps it below the trip point.

SRAM write. Drive one bitline to 0 and the other to V<sub>DD</sub> and raise WL. The access transistor on the 0 side must overpower the pMOS pull-up holding that node at 1, so the pull-up ratio (pull-up W/L ÷ access W/L) is kept small. When WL falls the loop holds the new value as long as power is on: no refresh.
1T1C DRAM structure. One access nMOS gated by WL connects the bitline to a storage capacitor C<sub>S</sub>. A 1 is stored as V<sub>DD</sub> on C<sub>S</sub>, a 0 as 0 V.

answer.text: DRAM read: precharge the bitline to V<sub>DD</sub>/2, raise WL, and let C<sub>S</sub> share charge with the bitline capacitance C<sub>BL</sub>. With C<sub>S</sub> = 30 fF, C<sub>BL</sub> = 270 fF and V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.2 V:
answer.pre:
ΔV = (V<sub>cell</sub> − V<sub>DD</sub>/2) × C<sub>S</sub> ÷ (C<sub>S</sub> + C<sub>BL</sub>)
   = (1.2 − 0.6) × 30 ÷ 300 = +60 mV   (stored 1)
   = (0 − 0.6) × 0.1 = −60 mV          (stored 0)
cell left at 0.66 V or 0.54 V: the bit is destroyed

answer: So the DRAM read is destructive: the sense amplifier latches the ±60 mV difference to full levels and drives the bitline back to 1.2 V or 0 V while WL is still high, which rewrites the cell (restore).

answer.text: DRAM retention and refresh. Leakage drains C<sub>S</sub>, so every row must be rewritten within t<sub>REF</sub>, typically 64 ms. For 8192 rows:
answer.pre:
row interval = 64 ms ÷ 8192 = 7.8125 µs
refresh rate = 8192 ÷ 64 ms = 128 rows per ms

answer.text: Comparison:

head: Property
6T SRAM
1T1C DRAM
rows: charge sharing, tens of mV, destructive, then restore

answer: Verdict: SRAM trades area for speed and simplicity; DRAM trades speed, refresh and a special process for density and cost per bit. Check: 1 Mbit of SRAM needs 6 × 2<sup>20</sup> = 6,291,456 transistors in its cells alone, against 2<sup>20</sup> transistors and capacitors for DRAM.

bank.q: Explain the D latch and the master-slave D flip-flop with a timing diagram. Define setup time, hold time and clock-to-Q delay.
outline: Positive latch transparent while CLK = 1, holds while CLK = 0: Q = CLK·D + CLK′·Q
Negative master + positive slave give a rising-edge register
Timing diagram: Q changes only just after rising edges
Setup and hold windows around the active edge
Clock-to-Q is the delay from edge to valid output; T ≥ t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>comb</sub> + t<sub>su</sub>
answer: D latch. A positive D latch is a 2:1 multiplexer with feedback: Q = CLK·D + CLK′·Q. While CLK = 1 it is transparent and Q follows D; while CLK = 0 the feedback path is selected and the cross-coupled inverters hold the last value. In CMOS: a transmission gate admits D when CLK = 1, a second transmission gate closes the inverter loop when CLK = 0, two inverters, eight transistors with the clock inverter left out.

Why a latch is not enough. Because it is transparent for a whole clock phase, a change of D, or a glitch, passes straight to Q while CLK = 1. Two latches on the same phase in series would let data race through both.

Master-slave register. Put a negative latch (the master, open while CLK = 0) before a positive latch (the slave, open while CLK = 1). While CLK = 0 the master follows D and the slave holds Q. At the rising edge the master closes on the value D had just before the edge and the slave opens and passes it to Q. While CLK = 1 the master is closed, so nothing new reaches Q. Q changes once per period, just after the rising edge.

answer.text: Timing diagram (draw these four waveforms; CLK rises at t = 2, 6 and 10, D rises at 1 and falls at 7):

answer: Reading the diagram: D fell at t = 7 while CLK was high, but Q fell only at the next rising edge, t = 10. That is edge-triggering.

Setup time t<sub>su</sub>: the time D must be stable before the clock edge, so the master has settled before it closes. Hold time t<sub>h</sub>: the time D must stay stable after the edge, so the closing master does not catch the new value. Clock-to-Q delay t<sub>cq</sub>: the time from the edge to a valid Q, mostly the slave latch's delay. Data changing inside the setup-hold window can leave the master metastable.

answer.text: Using them on a register-to-register path with t<sub>cq</sub> = 0.3 ns, logic t<sub>comb</sub> = 1.2 ns, t<sub>su</sub> = 0.15 ns, t<sub>h</sub> = 0.10 ns and T = 2 ns:
answer.pre:
setup slack = T − t<sub>cq</sub> − t<sub>comb</sub> − t<sub>su</sub> = 2 − 0.3 − 1.2 − 0.15 = 0.35 ns ≥ 0  passes
hold margin = t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>comb</sub> − t<sub>h</sub> = 0.3 + 1.2 − 0.10 = 1.4 ns ≥ 0  passes
T<sub>min</sub> = 0.3 + 1.2 + 0.15 = 1.65 ns,  f<sub>max</sub> = 1 ÷ 1.65 ns = 606.06 MHz

answer: Check: the hold equation has no T, so a hold failure cannot be cured by slowing the clock; the setup equation does, which is why f<sub>max</sub> comes from it.

bank.q: Draw the partial product array of a 4×4 Braun multiplier. Show where each full adder and half adder sits and estimate the worst-case delay in full-adder delays.
outline: AND gates form a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>j</sub> at fixed array positions: 16 for 4×4
Rows added from the top with carries going one row down and one column left
Half adders where a cell has no carry in: 4 HA and 8 FA, n(n−1) = 12 cells
Worst-case path: down the rows, then along the final ripple row
Delay about t<sub>AND</sub> + 2(n−1)t<sub>FA</sub> = t<sub>AND</sub> + 6t<sub>FA</sub>
answer: Partial products. For A = a<sub>3</sub>a<sub>2</sub>a<sub>1</sub>a<sub>0</sub> and B = b<sub>3</sub>b<sub>2</sub>b<sub>1</sub>b<sub>0</sub>, sixteen AND gates make pp<sub>ij</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>j</sub>, of weight 2<sup>i+j</sup>. Row j is A gated by b<sub>j</sub>, shifted j places left.

answer.text: Partial product array (columns by weight):

answer: Adder placement. p<sub>0</sub> = a<sub>0</sub>b<sub>0</sub> needs no adder. Row 1 of adders adds row b<sub>0</sub> to row b<sub>1</sub>: three cells with only two inputs each, so three half adders. Rows 2 and 3 of adders add rows b<sub>2</sub> and b<sub>3</sub>: each cell takes a partial product, the sum from above and a carry from the row above, so 2 × 3 = 6 full adders. Carries step one row down and one column left. A final row of 3 cells adds the remaining sum and carry bits: the first has two inputs (a half adder), the other two are full adders.

answer.text: Cell count:

answer: General count: n² AND gates, n(n−1) adder cells, of which n are half adders and n(n−2) full adders. For n = 4: 16, 12, 4 and 8.

Critical path. The slowest signal is formed by an AND gate, passes down the three adder rows (n − 1 = 3 adders, sum and carry outputs moving diagonally), and then ripples along the final row (n − 1 = 3 adders) to the top product bit p<sub>7</sub>. So t<sub>p</sub> ≈ t<sub>AND</sub> + 2(n − 1)t<sub>FA</sub> = t<sub>AND</sub> + 6t<sub>FA</sub>. With t<sub>AND</sub> = 30 ps and t<sub>FA</sub> = 100 ps that is 30 + 600 = 630 ps. The delay is linear in n, not n².
Check: 13 × 11 = 143 = 10001111<sub>2</sub>, 8 bits, as the array's 2n = 8 outputs p<sub>7</sub>…p<sub>0</sub> require.

bank.q: Using Baugh-Wooley, multiply the 4-bit two's complement numbers 1011 and 0110. Show the inverted partial product bits and the correction constants added in the array.
outline: Identify sign bits a₃ and b₃; values −5 and +6
Invert the 2(n−1) = 6 mixed sign partial products; keep the corner a₃b₃
Add 1s at bit n = 4 and bit 2n − 1 = 7
Complete the array addition and read the 8-bit product modulo 256
Explain why the array shape stays regular
answer: Values. A = 1011: a<sub>3</sub> = 1, a<sub>2</sub> = 0, a<sub>1</sub> = 1, a<sub>0</sub> = 1, so A = −8 + 2 + 1 = −5. B = 0110: b<sub>3</sub> = 0, b<sub>2</sub> = 1, b<sub>1</sub> = 1, b<sub>0</sub> = 0, so B = +6. Expected product −30.

Rule. In the 4 × 4 array, partial products with no sign bit (i, j ≤ 2) are normal a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>j</sub>. Those with exactly one sign bit, a<sub>3</sub>b<sub>j</sub> (j ≤ 2) and a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>3</sub> (i ≤ 2), are inverted (NAND gates). The corner a<sub>3</sub>b<sub>3</sub> has positive weight and stays normal. Then add 1 at bit n = 4 and 1 at bit 2n − 1 = 7, that is 2<sup>4</sup> + 2<sup>7</sup> = 144, and keep 8 bits.

answer.text: Rows (weights in brackets; inverted bits marked NOT):
Add the columns (as the array would):
answer.pre:
rows      8 + 6 + 12 + 56 = 82  = 0101 0010
correction         144        = 1001 0000
total              226        = 1110 0010
keep 8 bits: 226 (no carry beyond bit 7 here)

answer: Read the result. 11100010 has its top bit set, so as an 8-bit two's complement number it is 226 − 256 = −30. Check: (−5) × (+6) = −30.

Why it works. In A = −a<sub>3</sub>2<sup>3</sup> + Σa<sub>i</sub>2<sup>i</sup>, the terms a<sub>3</sub>b<sub>j</sub> and a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>3</sub> have negative weight. Writing −x = (1 − x) − 1 = NOT(x) − 1 turns each negative bit into an inverted positive bit plus a constant; the constants of all six terms add up, modulo 2<sup>8</sup>, to the two fixed 1s at bits 4 and 7. The corner a<sub>3</sub>b<sub>3</sub> is negative times negative, so it is positive and stays normal.

Regularity. The array keeps its n × n shape: the same 16 partial-product positions (10 AND, 6 NAND), the same n(n−1) = 12 adder cells, and two constant inputs. There are no sign-extension rows and no separate correction adder, so the layout and the diagonal carry path are the same as a Braun array.
Check by direct signed multiplication: −5 × 6 = −30, and −30 + 256 = 226 = 11100010. The array answer matches.

bank.q: A 16-bit adder is built from four 4-bit blocks. Apply carry skip to the blocks and derive the worst-case carry delay in terms of block carry delay and multiplexer delay. Compare with the plain ripple delay.
outline: Block propagate P = p₃p₂p₁p₀ (AND)
Bypass path through one multiplexer per block
Worst case = first block ripple + (n/k − 1) multiplexers + last block ripple
Compare against 16 one-bit carry delays
Best block size √(n·t<sub>mux</sub> ÷ 2t<sub>c</sub>)
answer: Structure. Four blocks of k = 4 bits each keep their ripple carry chain. Each block adds an AND gate forming P = p<sub>3</sub>p<sub>2</sub>p<sub>1</sub>p<sub>0</sub> of its own bits and a 2:1 multiplexer on its carry-out: if P = 1 the block's carry-in goes straight out; if P = 0 the ripple carry-out is used. Draw four ripple blocks in a row with the four multiplexers between them, the P signals as selects.

Why the bypass is safe. If every p<sub>i</sub> = 1 the block cannot generate or kill a carry, so its carry-out equals its carry-in, and taking it directly gives the same answer sooner. If any p<sub>i</sub> = 0, that bit generates or kills, the carry-out does not depend on the carry-in, and it is produced inside the block anyway.

Worst case. The carry is generated at bit 0 (block 0) and every later bit propagates. It ripples through block 0 (k bit delays), leaves through block 0's multiplexer, skips blocks 1 and 2 through their multiplexers, and ripples through block 3 (k bit delays) to the top bit. The multiplexers on the path number n/k − 1 = 3.

answer.text: With t<sub>c</sub> the carry delay of one bit and t<sub>mux</sub> one multiplexer delay:

answer: In terms of the block carry delay t<sub>block</sub> = k·t<sub>c</sub> = 4t<sub>c</sub>: T<sub>skip</sub> ≈ 2t<sub>block</sub> + 3t<sub>mux</sub>.

answer.text: Numbers, against a plain 16-bit ripple adder (16t<sub>c</sub>):

answer: Best block size. dT/dk = 2t<sub>c</sub> − n·t<sub>mux</sub> ÷ k² = 0 gives k<sub>opt</sub> = √(n·t<sub>mux</sub> ÷ 2t<sub>c</sub>). For n = 16 and t<sub>mux</sub> = t<sub>c</sub>, k<sub>opt</sub> = √8 ≈ 2.8, so blocks of 2 or 4: k = 2 gives 4 + 7 = 11 units too. Equal 4-bit blocks are already at the optimum for 16 bits.

Improvements. Using smaller blocks at the two ends and larger ones in the middle (variable block sizes), or a second level of skip, shortens the path further, because the long ripples are only at the ends.

Check: the saving grows with width. For 32 bits with k = 4 the same formula gives 8 + 7 = 15 units against 32 for ripple. Cost: four AND gates and four multiplexers, far less than carry select or look-ahead.

bank.q: Design a 3-to-8 decoder with an active-high enable using NAND gates. Use it and a few gates to realise f = Σm(1, 3, 5, 7) and state the gate count.
outline: Three inverters generate the complemented inputs
Eight 4-input NAND gates, one per minterm, each including the enable
Outputs are active-low: Ȳ<sub>i</sub> = 0 only for the selected line
OR of minterms = NAND of the active-low outputs Ȳ₁, Ȳ₃, Ȳ₅, Ȳ₇
Function reduces to f = C (with EN = 1), a useful check
answer: Literals. Inputs A (MSB), B, C and enable EN (active high). Three inverters give A′, B′ and C′, so every minterm can be formed.

answer.text: Decoder gates. Each output is a 4-input NAND of EN and three literals, so it is 0 (active-low) only for its own code while EN = 1:

answer: Enable. With EN = 0 every NAND has a 0 input, so all eight outputs are 1: no line is selected. With EN = 1 exactly one output is 0. Two such decoders, with A driving one EN directly and the other through an inverter, make a 4-to-16 decoder.

The function. f = m<sub>1</sub> + m<sub>3</sub> + m<sub>5</sub> + m<sub>7</sub> = Y<sub>1</sub> + Y<sub>3</sub> + Y<sub>5</sub> + Y<sub>7</sub>. The decoder gives Ȳ<sub>i</sub>, and by De Morgan, Y<sub>1</sub> + Y<sub>3</sub> + Y<sub>5</sub> + Y<sub>7</sub> = NOT(Ȳ<sub>1</sub>·Ȳ<sub>3</sub>·Ȳ<sub>5</sub>·Ȳ<sub>7</sub>). So one 4-input NAND of Ȳ<sub>1</sub>, Ȳ<sub>3</sub>, Ȳ<sub>5</sub>, Ȳ<sub>7</sub> gives f: a NAND-NAND realisation with no OR gate.

answer.text: Truth table check (EN = 1):

answer: Simplification check. f = 1 exactly when C = 1, so f = C (with EN = 1; f = 0 when EN = 0). In practice a single wire and an AND with EN would do; the decoder realisation is still asked because it works for any minterm list.

answer.text: Gate count:

answer: Check: every odd code (C = 1) pulls one of Ȳ<sub>1</sub>, Ȳ<sub>3</sub>, Ȳ<sub>5</sub>, Ȳ<sub>7</sub> low, which drives the output NAND high; every even code leaves all four high and f low.

bank.q: Build an 8:1 multiplexer from 2:1 multiplexers and show how the same structure fed by stored bits implements a 3-input lookup table for an FPGA logic cell.
outline: Tree of 2:1 stages, three select levels for eight inputs
Seven 2:1 multiplexers: 4 + 2 + 1
Delay about 3t<sub>mux</sub>
Lookup table: the truth table stored in 8 memory bits feeds the data inputs
Any 3-variable function by loading 8 bits; a 4-input LUT needs 16 bits and 15 multiplexers
answer: 2:1 multiplexer. Y = S′·D<sub>0</sub> + S·D<sub>1</sub>; in CMOS, two transmission gates driven by S and S′ (pass transistor logic).

Tree. Level 1: four 2:1 multiplexers select between D<sub>0</sub>/D<sub>1</sub>, D<sub>2</sub>/D<sub>3</sub>, D<sub>4</sub>/D<sub>5</sub>, D<sub>6</sub>/D<sub>7</sub> using the least significant select S<sub>0</sub>. Level 2: two multiplexers select between those pairs using S<sub>1</sub>. Level 3: one multiplexer selects using S<sub>2</sub>. Total 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 multiplexers; for N inputs, N − 1.

answer.text: Selection check for S<sub>2</sub>S<sub>1</sub>S<sub>0</sub> = 101:

answer: Delay. Every path passes ⌈log<sub>2</sub>8⌉ = 3 multiplexers: t<sub>pd</sub> ≈ 3t<sub>mux</sub>. With transmission gates the series resistance grows along the path, so long trees are buffered.

Lookup table. By Shannon expansion, any function of three variables equals a multiplexer whose selects are the variables and whose data inputs are the function's truth-table values. In an FPGA the data inputs come from 8 configuration memory cells (SRAM latches or flip-flops) loaded when the chip is configured, and the logic inputs A, B, C drive S<sub>2</sub>, S<sub>1</sub>, S<sub>0</sub>. The same cell becomes any of the 2<sup>8</sup> = 256 functions of three variables.

answer.text: Example: f = Σm(1, 2, 5, 7). Load:

answer: Check two inputs. ABC = 010 selects D<sub>2</sub> = 1, and 2 is a minterm of f. ABC = 110 selects D<sub>6</sub> = 0, and 6 is not. The table reproduces f for all eight codes because it is f.

Storage. The configuration cells are static latches, so the function survives with the clock stopped; a flip-flop after the multiplexer (with a bypass multiplexer) lets the cell be used as combinational or registered logic.

Scaling. A 4-input lookup table needs 2<sup>4</sup> = 16 stored bits and a 16:1 tree of 15 multiplexers (4 levels); a k-input one needs 2<sup>k</sup> bits, which is why commercial cells stop at about 4 to 6 inputs. Check for 3 inputs: 8 bits, 7 multiplexers, 3 levels.

bank.q: Compare ripple carry, carry look-ahead, carry select and carry skip adders for an N-bit word on area, delay and wiring complexity. Which would you choose at N = 64 and why?
outline: Delay order: ripple linear; skip and select about √N; hierarchical look-ahead logarithmic
Area order: ripple smallest, skip a little more, look-ahead and select largest
Wiring and layout regularity favour ripple, skip and select
Numbers for N = 64 in gate delays
Justified choice with the trade-off stated
answer: Common delay model. A full adder's carry takes 2 gate delays, a 2:1 multiplexer about 2 gate delays, an XOR 1. All numbers below are for N = 64 under this model; real designs differ in detail but keep the ranking.

Ripple carry. Delay 2N = 128 gate delays (carry-out). Area: N full adders, the minimum. Wiring: one cell repeated with only neighbour-to-neighbour connections. Fine for 8 bits, hopeless for a 64-bit datapath at GHz rates.

Carry skip. Delay T ≈ 2k·t<sub>c</sub> + (N/k − 1)·t<sub>mux</sub>. With t<sub>c</sub> = t<sub>mux</sub> = 2 gate delays, k<sub>opt</sub> = √(64 ÷ 2) ≈ 5.7; k = 4 gives 16 + 30 = 46 and k = 8 gives 32 + 14 = 46 gate delays. Area: ripple plus one AND and one multiplexer per block (about 8 to 16 multiplexers). Wiring: regular. Delay grows as √N.

Carry select (square-root). Blocks of 2, 3, 4, … 11 bits (sum 65 ≥ 64), so about 10 blocks. The first block ripples in 4 gate delays, and each later block's answers are ready as the selected carry arrives, so the carry-out is ready after about 4 + 9 × 2 = 22 gate delays, about 24 with the last sum multiplexer. Area: almost two adders plus N multiplexers. Wiring: regular but wide multiplexer select lines.

Carry look-ahead (hierarchical, 4-bit blocks). Three levels for 64 bits: g, p at 1; group signals at 3 and 5; top-level carries at 7; back down at 9 and 11; sums at 12 gate delays. Area: g/p logic, 16 + 4 + 1 look-ahead units with fan-in up to 5, and long wires between levels. Wiring: the most irregular, with high fan-out of the low-order signals.

answer.text: Summary for N = 64:

answer: Analysis. Going from ripple to skip removes most of the delay for a few per cent more area: the best speed-per-area step. Select halves the delay again by doubling the adder. Look-ahead halves it once more, but needs careful sizing and wiring; at 64 bits its logarithmic growth is what makes the difference, because every other scheme grows at least as √N.

Choice at N = 64. For a processor ALU on the critical path: a hierarchical look-ahead adder (in practice a parallel-prefix form of it), about 12 gate delays, about ten times faster than ripple. For an address incrementer, a low-power accelerator or anything off the critical path: carry skip, which gets within a factor of four of look-ahead at little more than ripple area. Carry select is a good middle choice when a regular layout matters more than area, and is often combined with look-ahead blocks.
Check: the ranking 128 > 46 > 24 > 12 gate delays follows the growth laws N > √N > log N, and the area ranking runs the other way, so the choice is an explicit speed-for-area trade.

bank.q: Compare an array multiplier with a Wallace tree multiplier for 16×16 bits on delay, area and layout regularity. Explain how Booth recoding changes the picture.
outline: Array: 256 AND gates, 240 adder cells, delay about t<sub>AND</sub> + 30t<sub>FA</sub>, regular
Wallace: 16 rows reduced in 6 levels, then a fast 32-bit adder
Counter count is similar; the tree costs long, irregular wires
Booth radix-4: 8 rows, 4 levels; extra recoding and selection logic
Recommendation depends on whether regularity or speed dominates
answer: Common ground. Both multiply 16 × 16 bits into a 32-bit product from the same 16 × 16 = 256 partial-product bits (AND gates, or NAND gates for the signed bits of Baugh-Wooley). They differ in how they add the 16 rows.

Array (Braun or Baugh-Wooley). n(n−1) = 16 × 15 = 240 adder cells in 15 rows, each row adding one more partial product, then a ripple row. Delay ≈ t<sub>AND</sub> + 2(n−1)t<sub>FA</sub> = t<sub>AND</sub> + 30t<sub>FA</sub>: linear in n. Layout: a rectangle of identical cells with nearest-neighbour wiring, easy to draw and to pipeline row by row.

answer.text: Wallace tree. Each level groups rows in threes and turns each group into two with carry save adders:

answer: Wallace delay. Six full-adder delays for the reduction, matching ⌈log<sub>1.5</sub>(16/2)⌉ = ⌈5.13⌉ = 6, then one 32-bit carry propagate adder. With a fast (look-ahead) final adder of roughly 12 gate delays, about 6 t<sub>FA</sub> at 2 gate delays per t<sub>FA</sub>, the total is about t<sub>AND</sub> + 12t<sub>FA</sub>, against t<sub>AND</sub> + 30t<sub>FA</sub> for the array: about 2.5 times faster.

Wallace area and layout. The tree uses about the same number of full adders as the array (each full adder removes one bit, and both must remove the same bits), plus a fast final adder. The cost is wiring: bits move between columns and levels in an irregular pattern, wires are long and cross, and the layout is harder to make compact.

Booth radix-4. Recode the multiplier into 8 digits from −2 to +2 by reading overlapping triplets; each partial product is 0, ±M or ±2M, chosen by a small selector (2M is a shift, −M an inversion plus a 1 added in the tree). Rows fall from 16 to 8 (plus sign-extension bits), so the Wallace tree needs 8 → 6 → 4 → 3 → 2, four levels instead of six, and about half the adders. In an array, Booth halves the height of the array and its delay.

answer.text: Estimates for 16 × 16:

answer: Evaluation. If speed matters (a processor or DSP multiplier on the critical path), Booth radix-4 with a Wallace or Dadda tree and a fast final adder is the standard answer: fewest levels and fewest adders. If regularity, low design effort or deep pipelining matter, or the multiplier is small, the array is attractive: it is easy to lay out, easy to pipeline and its delay is predictable.
Check: the level counts follow 16 → 11 → 8 → 6 → 4 → 3 → 2 (six levels) and 8 → 6 → 4 → 3 → 2 (four levels); Booth saves exactly the first two levels.

bank.q: A multiply-accumulate datapath has a 4.0 ns multiplier and a 2.0 ns adder between registers with t<sub>cq</sub> = 0.3 ns and t<sub>su</sub> = 0.2 ns. Analyse its clock rate and latency unpipelined, in two stages and in three balanced stages, and explain how clock skew between the pipeline registers can cause a hold violation.
outline: Unpipelined T = t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>logic</sub> + t<sub>su</sub>
Two stages limited by the slower stage; three balanced stages
Throughput against latency; (k + N − 1) periods for N inputs
Setup with skew: T + δ ≥ t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>logic</sub> + t<sub>su</sub>; hold: t<sub>cq,cd</sub> + t<sub>logic,cd</sub> ≥ t<sub>h</sub> + δ
Positive skew helps setup and can break hold; fix by delaying the short path
answer: Unpipelined. One register-to-register path holds both blocks: T = 0.3 + 4.0 + 2.0 + 0.2 = 6.5 ns, f = 1 ÷ 6.5 ns = 153.8 MHz, latency 6.5 ns.

Two stages (register after the multiplier). Stage delays 4.0 ns and 2.0 ns; the clock must suit the slower: T = 0.3 + 4.0 + 0.2 = 4.5 ns, f = 222.2 MHz. Latency 2 × 4.5 = 9.0 ns. The adder stage idles 2.0 ns of every period, so the gain is only 6.5 ÷ 4.5 = 1.44.

Three balanced stages (multiplier split into two 2.0 ns halves, for example the partial-product tree and the final adder). T = 0.3 + 2.0 + 0.2 = 2.5 ns, f = 400 MHz, latency 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 ns. Gain 6.5 ÷ 2.5 = 2.6, not 3, because each stage pays 0.5 ns of register overhead.

answer.text: Summary:

answer: Analysis. Pipelining raises throughput, not the speed of one sample: latency rises from 6.5 ns to 7.5 or 9.0 ns. Balancing the stages matters more than their number, and the overhead t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>su</sub> sets a floor: even infinitely many stages could not beat 0.5 ns per period.

Skew. Let δ = clock arrival at the capturing register − arrival at the launching register. The setup check becomes T + δ ≥ t<sub>cq</sub> + t<sub>logic,max</sub> + t<sub>su</sub>, so positive δ (clock routed with the data) lets T shrink: with δ = 0.15 ns, T ≥ 2.5 − 0.15 = 2.35 ns.

answer.text: Hold. The same edge that launches new data at one register must not let it reach the next register before that register's hold time has ended. Take t<sub>h</sub> = 0.1 ns, contamination delays t<sub>cq,cd</sub> = 0.2 ns and a shortest logic path t<sub>logic,cd</sub> = 0.1 ns (a bypass wire between two stages):
answer.pre:
hold: t<sub>cq,cd</sub> + t<sub>logic,cd</sub> ≥ t<sub>h</sub> + δ
δ = 0.15 ns:  0.2 + 0.1 = 0.30 ≥ 0.1 + 0.15 = 0.25   passes, margin 0.05 ns
δ = 0.25 ns:  0.30 ≥ 0.1 + 0.25 = 0.35                 fails by 0.05 ns

answer: Why skew causes it. With positive skew the capturing register is clocked later, so it is still holding when data launched at the earlier edge, through the short path, arrives: it captures the new value a cycle too early. T is not in the hold check, so slowing the clock does not help.

Fixes. Add delay to the short path only (a buffer of at least 0.05 ns, say 0.1 ns, gives 0.40 ≥ 0.35), reduce the skew by balancing the clock tree, or use registers with a smaller hold time. Adding the buffer leaves the long path, and so T, unchanged.
Check: with δ = 0.25 ns and a 0.1 ns buffer, setup T ≥ 2.5 − 0.25 = 2.25 ns and hold 0.40 ≥ 0.35 ns both pass, so the skew becomes a speed gain instead of a failure.

bank.q: A system needs 1 Mbit of on-chip storage and 1 Gbit of main memory. Evaluate the choice of 6T SRAM for the first and 1T1C DRAM for the second, covering cell size, speed, refresh, sense amplifier design and standby power.
outline: SRAM cell is six transistors, DRAM cell one transistor and one capacitor
SRAM read is differential, fast and non-destructive; DRAM needs charge sensing and restore
DRAM refresh costs bandwidth and standby power
Sense amplifiers and precharge differ: V<sub>DD</sub> against V<sub>DD</sub>/2
Conclusion: SRAM for speed-critical on-chip storage, DRAM for density
answer: Cell size. 1 Mbit of 6T SRAM needs 6 × 2<sup>20</sup> = 6,291,456 transistors in its cells. 1 Gbit of 6T SRAM would need 6 × 2<sup>30</sup> ≈ 6.44 billion, against 2<sup>30</sup> ≈ 1.07 billion transistors (plus capacitors) for 1T1C DRAM. The DRAM cell is far smaller, which is what makes a gigabit affordable.

Process. SRAM uses the ordinary logic transistors, so it sits on the processor die next to the logic. DRAM needs a large, low-leakage storage capacitor (trench or stacked) built in a special process, so gigabit DRAM is a separate chip.

Speed. SRAM reads differentially: BL and BLB start at V<sub>DD</sub>, the cell pulls one down, and a latch sense amplifier fires at about 0.1 V. With C<sub>BL</sub> = 100 fF and 40 µA of cell current that takes 100 fF × 0.1 V ÷ 40 µA = 0.25 ns. DRAM reads by charge sharing: the bitline starts at V<sub>DD</sub>/2 and moves only (V<sub>DD</sub>/2) × C<sub>S</sub> ÷ (C<sub>S</sub> + C<sub>BL</sub>), ±60 mV for 30 fF and 270 fF at 1.2 V, then the sense amplifier must amplify and restore before the row can close. Row cycles take tens of nanoseconds, so DRAM is slower per access.

Sense amplifier design. SRAM: one sense amplifier per column multiplexer output, fired by a replica-timed SE, with precharge to V<sub>DD</sub>. DRAM: a latch sense amplifier on every bitline pair of the open row, precharge and equalise to V<sub>DD</sub>/2, very tight offset because the signal is only tens of millivolts, and it doubles as the restore circuit after the destructive read.

answer.text: Refresh. A DRAM bit leaks away in milliseconds. With 8192 rows per bank and t<sub>REF</sub> = 64 ms:
answer.pre:
one row every 64 ms ÷ 8192 = 7.8125 µs
128 row refreshes every millisecond, each blocking that bank for one row cycle

answer: Refresh takes bandwidth from normal accesses and energy even when the system is idle. SRAM never refreshes.

Standby power. An SRAM cell leaks through its off transistors all the time, so a large SRAM has high standby leakage per bit. DRAM leaks very little per cell but pays refresh power. At 1 Mbit the SRAM leakage is acceptable; at 1 Gbit SRAM leakage and area would both be prohibitive.

answer.text: Evaluation:

answer: Verdict: both choices are right. SRAM gives the on-chip store sub-nanosecond, refresh-free access in the logic process; DRAM gives the main memory about six times fewer transistors per bit and a gigabit at a sensible cost, paying with slower destructive reads and refresh. Check: 6 × 2<sup>30</sup> ÷ 2<sup>30</sup> = 6 transistors against 1 per bit.

bank.q: Classify the timing schemes of digital systems. Explain self-timed design with the four-phase handshake, dual-rail completion detection and the Muller C-element.
outline: Synchronous, mesochronous, plesiochronous, asynchronous: clocks and phase relation
Interfaces: phase adjust, elastic buffer, synchronizer
Four-phase handshake: Req↑, Ack↑, Req↓, Ack↓
Dual-rail coding with a spacer; completion when every bit pair has one rail high
C-element truth table and its use in a Muller pipeline; merits and costs

answer.text: Classification:

head: Class
Clocks
Phase
Interface needed
rows: phase adjustment (delay line or small FIFO)
elastic buffer that occasionally drops or repeats a word
synchronizer (two flip-flops) into a clocked domain, or handshakes

answer: Self-timed idea. Instead of a clock that must suit the slowest path, each stage signals when its output is valid. Timing becomes local: a stage starts as soon as its input is ready and its successor is free, so the system runs at the actual (average) data delay.

Four-phase handshake. Sender puts data on the bus and raises Req (1). Receiver takes the data and raises Ack (2). Sender lowers Req (3). Receiver lowers Ack (4), ready for the next transfer. Data must stay valid from event 1 until event 2. Draw Req and Ack as two overlapping pulses, Ack shifted right, with the data valid window above them and the four events numbered.

answer.text: Dual-rail coding. Each bit uses two wires (t, f):

answer: Completion detection. Bit i is complete when t<sub>i</sub> + f<sub>i</sub> = 1 (an OR gate). The word is complete when all bits are: the OR outputs are joined by a tree of C-elements, whose output becomes the Req to the next stage. Between words all rails return to the spacer, so the detector sees a fresh 0 → 1 for every word. Example for the 2-bit value 10: bit 1 = (1, 0), bit 0 = (0, 1), both ORs are 1, so "done" rises.

answer.text: Muller C-element: output Z follows the inputs only when they agree:

answer: Trace: from Z = 0, inputs (1, 0) → 0; (1, 1) → 1; (0, 1) → 1 (an AND gate would have fallen); (0, 0) → 0. CMOS: two series pMOS and two series nMOS to an output node held by a weak keeper. In a Muller pipeline each stage's C-element takes the previous stage's request and the inverted output of the next stage's C-element, so a token moves forward only when the next stage is empty.
Merits. No clock tree, clock power or skew; average-case speed; robust to supply, temperature and process variation; modular composition.

Costs. Dual rail doubles the data wires and adds completion detectors; logic must be hazard-free; testing and tool support are weaker. Bundled data (single-rail data plus a matched delay line on Req) is cheaper but must be margined like a clock.
Check: in a four-phase transfer each of Req and Ack rises once and falls once, four events in all, and the C-element is the only gate needed to wait for two such events at once.

bank.q: Organise a 2 Mbit SRAM as 256K words × 8 bits with a nearly square core. Find the row and column address bits, design the row decoder with predecoding, and estimate the bitline sensing time for C<sub>BL</sub> = 150 fF, a 30 µA cell current and a 120 mV sense margin.
outline: K = 18 address bits for 256K words
Core 1024 rows × 2048 columns: r = 10, columns = 8 × 2<sup>c</sup>, c = 8
Row decoder: two 5-to-32 predecoders and 1024 two-input gates
Column decoder and 256:1 multiplexer per data bit; 8 sense amplifiers
Sensing time t = C<sub>BL</sub>ΔV ÷ I against a full swing
answer: Size. 256K = 2<sup>18</sup> words, so K = 18 address bits. Total cells: 2<sup>18</sup> × 8 = 2<sup>21</sup> = 2,097,152 = 2 Mbit.

Shape. √(2<sup>21</sup>) ≈ 1448 is not a power of two, so choose 2<sup>10</sup> × 2<sup>11</sup>: 1024 rows by 2048 columns (shorter bitlines, 1024 cells each) rather than 2048 rows by 1024 columns (bitlines twice as long and slower).

answer.text: Address split:
answer.pre:
rows    = 2<sup>r</sup> = 1024            → r = 10
columns = M × 2<sup>c</sup> = 8 × 2<sup>c</sup> = 2048 → 2<sup>c</sup> = 256 → c = 8
check   r + c = 10 + 8 = 18 = K

answer: Each row holds 256 words of 8 bits. The 8 column bits drive a column decoder whose 256 select lines operate eight 256:1 column multiplexers, one per data bit, each feeding one sense amplifier and one write driver. A 256:1 one-level multiplexer loads its output heavily, so it is usually built in two levels, 16:1 then 16:1.

rows: 16 gates, and each predecoded line drives 32

answer: Predecoding cuts gate inputs by 10240 ÷ 2368 ≈ 4.3 and makes each wordline gate a 2-input NAND plus a driver inverter that fits the cell pitch. Address bits A<sub>17</sub>–A<sub>13</sub> feed one predecoder, A<sub>12</sub>–A<sub>8</sub> the other, and A<sub>7</sub>–A<sub>0</sub> the column decoder.

answer: The latch sense amplifier therefore saves 5.0 − 0.6 = 4.4 ns per read. Its enable should come from a replica bitline so that it fires at about 120 mV in every process corner, and the bitlines must be precharged to V<sub>DD</sub> and equalised before each access.

Block diagram to draw: address register; row predecoders and 1024 wordline drivers on the left; the 1024 × 2048 core; precharge across the top; column multiplexers, 8 sense amplifiers and write drivers below; column decoder; data I/O; timing control (CE, WE, SE).
Check: 1024 rows × 256 words per row = 262,144 = 256K words, and 2048 columns ÷ 8 bits = 256 words per row, so every address maps to exactly one 8-bit word.

glossary.def: A multiplier built as a regular two-dimensional array of AND gates and adders.
A two's complement array multiplication scheme using bit inversion and correction constants to keep the array regular.
The column wire that carries the stored bit from the selected cell to the sense amplifier.
A carry computed for a group of bits using that group's generate and propagate terms.
Recoding the multiplier bits into signed digits so that fewer partial products are needed.
Computing carries in parallel from generate and propagate signals instead of waiting for them to ripple.
A structured full-adder array that reduces three numbers to two without resolving carries.
An adder that precomputes sums for both possible carry inputs and selects one with a multiplexer.
An adder block that bypasses the carry straight to the next block when every bit only propagates.
The fixed difference in arrival time of the same clock edge at two registers.
A circuit that reports whether two binary words are equal, or which one is larger.
A multiplier that uses the minimum number of counters at each stage, at the cost of irregular wiring.
A circuit that asserts exactly one of 2ⁿ outputs for each n-bit input code.
An edge-triggered storage element that samples data only at a clock transition.
A two-input circuit producing a sum bit a ⊕ b and a carry bit ab.
A level-sensitive storage element that is transparent for half the clock period.
A dynamic chain of pass transistors that propagates or kills a carry along a block.
The unresolved state a storage element may enter when its input changes inside the setup-hold window.
A gate whose output follows its inputs only when they agree and holds otherwise; used to join handshakes in self-timed circuits.
A selector that connects one of several inputs to a single output under select control.
The shifted multiplicand row produced by one multiplier bit before the rows are summed.
Inserting registers into long logic so a new input can start every short clock period; raises throughput at the cost of latency.
A small decoder for a group of address bits whose outputs are combined by 2- or 3-input gates to drive each wordline.
Periodic rewriting of DRAM cells to replace charge lost by leakage.
An odd number of inverters connected in a loop, oscillating at 1 ÷ (2N·t<sub>p</sub>).
Passing the carry out of one adder stage into the next, so carries travel through the whole word.
A switching circuit with two thresholds, whose hysteresis turns a slow or noisy input into one clean edge.
A small cross-coupled amplifier that resolves the weak bitline signal into a full logic level.
A tree of 3:2 counters that reduces partial product rows to two in logarithmic depth.
The row wire a decoder drives to connect a whole row of memory cells to their bitlines.
